newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan says Cyprus talks going "reasonably well".
newsitem.headline: Annan says Cyprus talks going "reasonably well".

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Friday talks between the leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities were going "reasonably well."
It was the first comment by any U.N. official since Annan presided over the opening of five days of negotiations Wednesday between President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.
Asked by Reuters how the talks, due to end on Sunday, were proceeding, the secretary-general replied: "Reasonably well. They are still talking and as long as they are talking we are making progress."

Asked to confirm that a second round would take place near Geneva Aug. 11-16, he said, "This is something that we will firm up at the end of the talks. But we do expect to have another round in Europe."
Clerides and Denktash are discussing how to revive long-stalled efforts to reunite their divided island as a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.
Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since troops from Turkey took over the north of the island in 1974 in reaction to a coup in Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece.

After Wednesday's opening session Annan handed over to his special adviser for Cyprus, former Ecuadorean Foreign Minister Diego Cordovez, who held a series of separate and joint meetings with the two Cypriot leaders.

Cordovez was reported to have given them suggestions designed to facilitate their work. But no details were disclosed and the United Nations clamped a news blackout on the talks to try to prevent the two long-time rivals from sniping at each other through the media.

Clerides and Denktash were also reported to have met alone several times, taking walks together around the picturesque rural resort, called Troutbeck, where they are staying, 90 miles (145 kms) north of New York city.

Annan told the opening meeting he believed that "a lasting peace in Cyprus is now within our grasp." But he also said the consequences of failure "are likely to be more dire than at any time in recent decades."
He was apparently alluding to forthcoming events that could precipitate a crisis.

These include talks expected to begin in 1998 on European Union membership for Cyprus, which the Turkish Cypriots oppose unless negotiated by a government in which they are partners; and the Greek Cypriot-led government's plan to deploy Russian-made S-300 air defence missiles next year, which Turkey vowed to prevent.
